title: Short Stuff: The Voice of God
summary: Short Stuff episode on Don LaFontaine, the voice actor known as "the Voice of God" and "the movie trailer guy." The hosts cover his early career as a recording engineer in the US Army Band and at National Recording Studios, his 1962 partnership with producer Floyd Peterson, the 1965 MGM Gunfighters of Casa Grande radio spots that led to a buyout, his coining or popularizing of trailer catchphrases such as "In a world..." and "nowhere to run, nowhere to hide," his 1976 production company, his 1978 move to Paramount to run its trailer department, his 1981 move to Los Angeles, his dominance of network and cable promos and award-show announcing, his 2005 Geico commercial, his smoking history, his death from a pulmonary embolism in September 2008 at age 68, his burial at Hollywood Forever Cemetery, his final role in a Phineas and Ferb episode, and the question of whether he has a Hollywood Walk of Fame star. The episode also includes off-topic banter about voiceover work, the film Disclosure Day, the movie In a World, and AI assistant errors.

segments.title: Opening and introduction
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the Short Stuff episode about Don LaFontaine, the voice known as the Voice of God.

segments.title: LaFontaine's prolific output
segments.summary: The hosts note LaFontaine recorded more than 5,000 movie trailers and about 70,000 TV spots, and was averaging seven voiceovers a day near the end of his life.

segments.title: Difficulty of voiceover work
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how demanding voiceover recording is, comparing it to their own audiobook reading.

segments.title: Early career and MGM buyout
segments.summary: LaFontaine was born in Duluth, Minnesota, served in the US Army Band and Chorus as a recording engineer, and worked at National Recording Studios in New York. In 1962 he partnered with producer Floyd Peterson. In 1965 he filled in on radio spots for the Gunfighters of Casa Grande, and MGM bought the work outright.

segments.title: Modern movie trailer and catchphrases
segments.summary: The hosts describe how LaFontaine and Peterson helped develop the modern movie trailer, with Floyd L. Peterson, Inc. formed as a company. LaFontaine is credited with popularizing catchphrases such as 'In a world,' 'nowhere to run, nowhere to hide,' and 'no way out.'

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Brief break before the hosts continue the segment.

segments.title: Parodies and Paramount years
segments.summary: The catchphrase was widely parodied, including in Geico commercials and The Simpsons Movie. LaFontaine started Don LaFontaine Associates in 1976 with Godfather Part II as his first assignment, then joined Paramount in 1978 to run its trailer department. The hosts discuss Paramount's mountain logo.

segments.title: Off-topic movie banter
segments.summary: The hosts briefly discuss seeing the Spielberg film Disclosure Day.

segments.title: Move to Los Angeles and agent Steve Tisherman
segments.summary: LaFontaine left Paramount in 1981 and moved to Los Angeles. Agent Steve Tisherman encouraged him to focus on voiceover work, which cemented his legacy as a voiceover performer.

segments.title: Network and brand voice work
segments.summary: From the 1980s LaFontaine became the in-house voice for the four major US networks plus UPN, as well as TNT, TBS, and Cartoon Network. He also announced some Academy Awards shows. The hosts note his sense of humor.

segments.title: Geico commercial and Geico advertising
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a 2005 Geico commercial in which LaFontaine narrated a customer's claim story, and mention the Geico Caveman and a short-lived Geico TV show.

segments.title: Death, smoking history, and burial
segments.summary: LaFontaine was an on-and-off smoker who quit for two decades. He was admitted to Cedars-Sinai in 2008 with a pulmonary embolism and died September 1, 2008, at age 68. He is interred at Hollywood Forever Cemetery, which the hosts have covered before.

segments.title: Final performance and In a World film
segments.summary: The hosts say LaFontaine's last performance was in a Phineas and Ferb episode, 'The Chronicles of Meep,' where his final line was 'In a world... I said it, happy.' They also mention Lake Bell's 2013 film In a World about voiceover work.

segments.title: Walk of Fame star and AI errors
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether LaFontaine has a Hollywood Walk of Fame star. Chuck agrees to look it up, and they joke about AI assistant mistakes and a fake AI image of a star.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the Short Stuff episode, and the standard iHeartRadio credit is read.
